# Phosphorescence-based O 2 sensing reveals size-dependent survival and motility of metastatic prostate cancer cells in self-generated hypoxia

**Authors:** Noreen Hosny; Kimberly Shen; Yihua Zhao; Junle Qu; Yusha Sun; George Butler; Sarah Amend; Emma U. Hammarlund; Robert Gatenby; Joel Brown; Kenneth J. Pienta; Trung V. Phan; Stephano Boyer-Paulet; Shengkai Li; Robert H. Austin

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 2Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 3College of Physics and Optoelectronic Engineering, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China | 4Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Baltimore, MD, USA | 5Lund University Cancer Centre, Lund, Sweden | 6Moffitt Cancer Centre, Tampa, FL, USA

## Abstract

Cancer cells in solid tumors experience hypoxia, a condition of low O 2 concentration, since their O 2 demand exceeds the supply from the surrounding vasculature. However, how these cells adapt to hypoxia requires further elucidation. Here, we use a transparent phosphorescent thin film to visualize the self-generated hypoxia field of prostate cancer cells and quantify local O 2 consumption rates, measured locally as the Laplacian of the O 2 field. Single-cell tracking on steep O 2 gradients revealed that larger cells exhibit higher motility and moderate migration bias toward O 2 -rich regions. Termination of hypoxia before cessation of O 2 consumption shifted cell distributions to larger sizes, whereas prolonged hypoxia induced apoptosis, producing cell populations of smaller areas post-hypoxia. Such resilience to hypoxia was absent for noncancerous fibroblasts. Our findings suggest that larger PC3 cells have enhanced metabolic fitness under hypoxia, identifying these cells as potential targets of cancer therapy.

## Introduction

Hypoxia in tissue is defined as O 2 concentrations below those that are physiologically normal (normoxia), roughly below 2% atmospheric O 2 concentration. Hypoxic conditions in complex multicellular organisms are highly spatially heterogeneous and not necessarily an aberrant condition; for example, there exist physiological niches that have low O 2 concentrations such as stem cell niches,1 where cells have adapted to hypoxia and even require it for their biological function.2

Hypoxia can also exist at the core of solid malignant tumors,3,4 as its rapid growth leads to a disorganized vascular system that inefficiently supplies nutrients and O 2 .5,6,7,8 As a result, solid tumor cancer cells adapt to a chronic level of hypoxia8 by metabolizing nutrients using aerobic Warburg fermentation, resulting in the fermentation of glycerol into lactic acid.9 Although this process has a low yield of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), it has the advantage of converting nutrients, such as glucose and glutamine, more efficiently into the biomass needed for growth by avoiding unnecessary catabolic oxidation of such nutrients into carbon dioxide.

However, this chronic, self-generated deep hypoxia can become an existential threat even for cancer cells running the Warburg cycle—a self-generated crisis for tumor cells. In fact, Warburg fermentation in hypoxia is a two-edged sword in that while the substrates of the cell mass are efficiently generated by the Warburg process,10 the by-products of Warburg fermentation create an acidic microenvironment. Furthermore, the low level of ATP generated by Warburg fermentation means that important aspects of cell behavior, such as motility, are greatly curtailed in severe hypoxia.11,12 Thus, the adaptation of cancer cells to these stressful conditions is necessary for cell survival.

Although the mechanisms by which hypoxic tumor core cancer cells acquire fitness advantages for survival remain unclear, recent research has found that a subset of cancer cells, termed polyaneuploid cancer cells (PACCs), can adapt remarkably well to stressors such as chemotherapy treatment.13 PACCs are large, endoreplicative cells that emerge when aneuploid parent cells exit the normal cell cycle to complete multiple S phases without entry into the M phase.13,14,15,16,17 This results in physically large cells with increased and abnormal genomic content.

Here, we investigate the response of metastatic prostate cancer cells as a function of their size to extreme hypoxia in an effort to characterize the fitness of larger (and presumably polyaneuploid) cancer cells to hypoxia and compare their response to hypoxia with human stromal fibroblast cells. First, we assess the motility of metastatic PC3 cells in a self-generated hypoxic environment as a function of cell size. Second, we determine whether size-dependent motility is biased toward the O 2 gradient, suggesting that escape from the hypoxic core is a possible mechanism of adaptation. Finally, we assess whether survival of these cancer cells is size-dependent by determining the cell-area distributions of cancer cells subjected to different durations of hypoxia.

We aim to assess these objectives using a membrane-based culture system that allows cells, both PC3 metastatic prostate cancer cells and human stromal fibroblast cells, to self-generate a severe hypoxic environment (defined as levels of 10 − 3 normoxic conditions),18 closely similar to the process that occurs naturally in tumors. The system includes a thin film that is phosphorescent, allowing local O 2 concentrations to be spatially monitored and quantified throughout the duration of hypoxia. Self-generated hypoxia must be contrasted with the creation of pseudohypoxic conditions using cobalt chloride19 or by purging the O 2 environment. The cobalt chloride method is merely mimetic: it induces a hypoxia-like response in cells by stabilizing certain protein factors but does not physically decrease ambient O 2 levels.20 Furthermore, both cobalt chloride and O 2 purging are externally imposed rather than emergent from the tumor itself, creating uncertainty in the applicability of observed cell responses to the behavior of cells in vivo within tumors.

We have developed a membrane-based culture system that allows self-generation of hypoxia over time. As shown in Figure 1A, GFP-expressing prostate cancer cells (PC3-GFP cell line) in a gas-permeable plate rest under an acrylic plug. Using this system, we performed three sets of experiments: in one set, we remove self-imposed severe hypoxia before cessation of O 2 consumption and apoptotic blebbing to assess the impact of hypoxia on stressed cells. In another set, we allow severe hypoxia to proceed until O 2 consumption ceases and apoptosis-induced blebbing is evident for most cells. We then track the few cells that survive. In the third set, we examine the survival of a confluent layer of non-cancerous human stromal fibroblasts under conditions of self-induced hypoxia, providing a comparative analysis against cancer cells under the same conditions.

### Quantification of O 2 gradients and directed cell migration

We used the O 2 sensor film to determine three local parameters of O 2 : (1) the absolute local O 2 concentration ϕ ( r , t ) , (2) the gradient in the O 2 concentration, ∇ ϕ ( r , t ) , and (3) the local O 2 Laplacian, − D ∇ 2 ϕ , which can be related to the O 2 consumption rate of the cells (see STAR Methods).

A key area of investigation focuses on whether the direction of displacement of PC3 cells exhibits any correlation with the local O 2 gradients surrounding the cells, once conditions of stable and severe hypoxia are established in the central region of the culture system. Previous work in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research21 indicated that this aerotactic migration is prevalent among cancer cells confined under a glass slide, although we are concerned about the large hydrodynamic flow profiles in their procedure, which could lead to apparent cell movement due to hydrodynamic entrainment; however, this is not present in our protocol.

In our case, we measure the vector r → of a given cell displacement between two frames separated by 0.5 h in time and the calculated vector field gradient ∇ ϕ ( r ) of O 2 at that position. The normalized vector dot product ⟨ cos θ ⟩ gives a measure of movement along the O 2 gradient:(Equation 1) ⟨ cos θ ⟩ = 〈 ∇ ϕ ( r ) · r → | ∇ ϕ ( r ) | | r → | 〉

### O 2 calibration measurements

Although the most direct way to measure the local N concentration of excited triplet state molecules is through time-resolved single-photon counting histograms of N T ( t ) after an impulse excitation, as can be done with a Becker&Hickl DCS-120 confocal scanning PLIM, accurate measurements of local hypoxia levels can also be obtained by measuring the quasi-steady-state emission of the custom phosphorescent film during green excitation of the mCh filter set.

This is possible since the phosphorescence is red-shifted in the triplet state from the singlet fluorescence and the crossing of the PtTFPP is almost 100% singlet-triplet and does not interfere with the singlet state. Figure 2A shows the excitation and phosphorescence emission spectra of the PtTFPP film and the excitation and emission bands of the Nikon mCh filter set 3569115.

Figure 2B (reproduced from Figure 1B) shows the raw unprocessed emission of the dye film as it develops, as discussed later. We used the calibrations in Figures 2C and 2D in all subsequent images to create profiles of O 2 concentrations vs. time and space.

Calibration measurements were performed by exposing the PtTFPP/PFPE sensor to known concentrations of O 2 using a gas mixer to obtain different ratios of O 2 to Ar and taking images of the sensor phosphorescence intensity through the mCherry filter. We used a fixed exposure time ( 500 m sec ) and subtracted background counts (36/pixel), which were obtained by taking a blank image without excitation.

We have shown in a previous paper22 that the phosphorescence lifetime of the excited triplet state N ( t ) of PtTFPP is quenched at a diffusion limit by O 2 molecules. For steady state illumination of the film, if N T is the number of excited triplet molecules, N o is the total number of molecules, k p is the excitation rate of unexcited triplet molecules by the microscope illumination source, and k q is the quenching rate of excited triplet molecules by a concentration C of O 2 molecules, then the decay rate of triplet molecules is(Equation 3) d N T d t = − k o N T − k q N T C + k P ( N o − N T )

In steady state, d N T d t = 0 and the intensity I of the emitted phosphorescence I = − k o N T . Solving for I we get the following:(Equation 4) I = k p N o 1 + k q k o C + k p k o

If C = 0 , then I o is the intrinsic phosphorescence intensity in the absence of O 2 :(Equation 5) I o = k p N o 1 + k p k o

This yields(Equation 6) I = I o A A + C where A = ( 1 + k p k o ) k o k q . Since A is a constant, it can be treated as a curve fitting parameter. The intensity I of the emitted light measured in counts/pixel for a given exposure time can be used to directly determine the local O 2 concentration C .

Letting M indicate camera counts/pixel (with background counts already subtracted), we can then write M ( C ′ ) = α β + C ′ where C ′ is the O 2 concentration normalized to a value of 1 for 100%. The results of the calibration measurements and the curve fit generated by MATLAB’s curve fitting toolbox are given in the log(Counts/pixel) vs. log(C′) plot in Figure 2D. Fit values are α = 2.5 ± 0.4 and β = 0.0014 ± 0.0003. For different actual exposure times the counts/pixel were adjusted to the value expected for a 500 msec exposure.

### Removal of self-induced hypoxic conditions before cessation of O 2 consumption

In this experiment, self-induced hypoxia was stopped at +16 h by removing the acrylic plug. At that time, the O 2 concentration ϕ was low at ∼ 10 − 3 ϕ bar and did not change with time. We also observed at +16 h that cell O 2 consumption, as proxied by the local O 2 Laplacian value − D ∇ 2 ϕ , was slightly negative in the region of highest hypoxia at ∼ 10 − 14 moles/cm3 − sec and not changing with time. In particular, a “negative” flux indicates that local O 2 concentrations are increasing in that region. However, due to the concurrent processes of reaction and diffusion occurring locally, this does not imply that the cells are actively producing O 2 . In fact, we cannot completely disentangle the contributions of reaction and diffusion. Nonetheless, this experiment yields a strong hypoxic stress event, although not severe enough to kill the PC3 cells.

### Prostate Cancer Cell Migration in O 2 Gradients

If motility is apparent, the gradient of the O 2 concentration ∇ ϕ ( r , t ) could provide a vector to guide cell movement. Given the severe hypoxia generated in the core region, we hypothesize that cells would tend to move toward higher O 2 concentrations by following local O 2 gradients through aerotactic migration.

We computed the vector gradient of the O 2 concentration ∇ ϕ ( x , y ) as it developed. Figure 4C shows our computed gradients in O 2 levels as a function of time. The gradient increases in magnitude from the outside, reaching a maximum at the perimeter of disc and falling near the covered area due to cell O 2 consumption.

### Larger prostate cancer cells tend to exhibit greater motility in self-generated hypoxia

Under the assumption that the region of greatest O 2 consumption at the start of hypoxia development will also be the region of highest cell displacement, we measured the net integrated cell displacement during the first 1.5 h of hypoxia in the region of highest O 2 consumption as a function of cell diameter (Figures 4D, 4E, and 4F). For the PC3 cells under this self-generated hypoxic condition, we found that the integrated displacement increased with cell size, then became constant, with an increase in displacement only for the infrequent very large cells (Figures 4E and 4F).

A possible basis for the connection between cell motility and cell size can be explored using analogies to the Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics plot of enzyme activity vs. substrate concentration,24 and the double reciprocal Lineweaver-Burk plot.25 Following that lead, in Figure 4F, we plot 1/(integrated speed) of the cells vs. 1/length of the cells. We assume that total mitochondrial-derived cell O 2 consumption in terms of power U scales with the volume of the cell, so U ∼ α L 3 , where α is some power/volume in terms of O 2 consumption and L is the length of a hypothetical cubical cell (we avoid the analogy of spherical cells). We assume that this net energy/time under hypoxia is dissipated in three ways: (1) via the power necessary to drag the cell across a surface P D , (2) through molecular motor proteins, which play an important role in metabolism; these proteins bind to a polarized cytoskeletal filament and use the energy derived from repeated cycles of ATP hydrolysis to move steadily along the cytoskeleton, and (3) via the maintenance of the electrochemical difference across the cell membrane. Even in the absence of active work, a live cell must maintain a concentration gradient across the membrane due to leakage of molecules across the membrane. This is what is meant by resting potential, and maintenance of it is an active process requiring metabolism.26

Although adherent PC3 cells deform to form non-spherical (and certainly non-cubic) objects, we can assume that the thickness t of the cell also scales as some scalar value η < 1 of the diameter L of the flattened cells; that is, the volume V ∼ L 2 × η L = η L 3 . If we assume that the power drag P D is proportional to the normal force N of the cell buoyant weight (which scales as L 3 ) times the speed v , and that active motor entropy change scales with the area of the cell membrane L 2 times v , and the resting pump power is constant at a level δ L 2 , we obtain the following:(Equation 7) α L 3 ∼ β L 3 v + γ L 2 v + δ L 2 where α , β , γ , δ are the respective scaling factors of mitochondria power, hydrodynamic drag power, motor entropy power, and resting pump power. This yields(Equation 8) 1 v ∼ β + γ / L α − δ / L

A plot of 1 / v vs. 1 / L as shown in Figure 4F gives a good fit to a straight line, indicating that a significant metabolic cost to the cell in severe hypoxia is movement and that the net cost scales inversely with the cell diameter. Attempts to quantitatively model cell metabolism are difficult,27 and at this point we can simply state that attempts to escape severe hypoxia favor large cells based on our O 2 consumption measurements, which serve as a proxy to metabolism to a certain extent.

The intercept of Equation 8 for infinite L is the maximum speed that a cell can move when most energy is expended in kinetic drag. Of more biological interest is the slope of the Lineweaver-Burk plot, γ α , which has units of time and is a measure of the ratio of energy loss due to motor protein power to total mitochondria power. Since our measurement is done by single-cell tracking, we do not need to know the cell density to convert the slope to (in principle) obtain information on single-cell O 2 consumption in hypoxia. Our measured value of γ α is approximately 0.7 ± 0.1 hours. Although we have an estimate of α from the Laplacian analysis of the O 2 consumption of the cells, much work needs to be done to extract real biological metabolic information. The point remains, and larger cells move faster in severe hypoxia.

### Larger prostate cancer cells exhibit a moderate tendency to migrate toward higher O 2 concentrations

Within the region characterized by a steep O 2 gradient under hypoxic conditions, the largest cells (defined as having areas exceeding ∼ 2 , 000 μ m 2 ) demonstrated the most pronounced directional migration toward the O2 gradient (Figures 5A–5C). This behavior was quantified by a moderate Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence value of 0.0603 relative to the probability distribution denoted in red in Figures 5B–5E. In contrast, smaller cells (less than ∼ 2 , 000 μ m 2 in area) exhibited a lower KL divergence of 0.0159, indicating a reduced directional movement along the O2 gradient (Figure 5B). These findings suggest that larger cells exhibit a moderate degree of aerotactic migration along the O 2 gradients present in hypoxic environments. ### Changes in cell area during and after extreme hypoxia with no O 2 consumption

The culture system was constructed so that the cells were confined to a 50- μ m high ceiling. PC3 cells are highly adherent to surfaces; they generally only lift up for division or death. Adherent cells have a distinct morphology when they are adherent, and given the low ceiling, the cell area is a good, but not perfect, proxy for the volume. Future work may employ confocal imaging to better measure cell volume.

In this experiment, there was no sign of apoptosis (blebbing) after 16 h of hypoxia, and full O 2 consumption was maintained based on the stability of the hypoxia region. After stopping hypoxia by removal of the plug, we tracked the cells to assess their survival using the Cellpose framework outlined in STAR Methods. To do this, we determined both the cell number N s and the cell size A s after hypoxia removal. Cell number N s was a measure of the number of adherent cells attached to the surface after hypoxia removal, and tracking cell area A s was predicated on the previous result that large cells had a bias toward moving up O 2 gradients.

Figure 6A shows the cell area distribution after hypoxia was removed as a function of time during and after hypoxia removal within the hypoxia region alone. As shown in Figure 6A, during the 16 h course of hypoxia, the log-normal distribution of cell areas shifted to larger sizes, suggesting that larger cells are more resistant to severe hypoxia than smaller cells. Once hypoxia was removed, there was a decrease in the total number of adherent cells (Figures 6B and 6C) within the hypoxia region. ### Non-cancerous human stromal fibroblasts lack resilience to self-generated hypoxia

Removal of hypoxia by lifting the plug at 16 h into hypoxia, where PC3 cells would still be viable and propagate, gave a dramatically different response for HSF cells. Most of the cells detached with plug removal with continual loss over 10 h, as shown in the ridgeline plot of Figure 10C. Continued culturing resulted in no cell regrowth (data not shown). Hence, unlike PC3 cells, the HSF cells were generally killed at the hypoxia levels that PC3 cells survived. This underscores the relative resilience of cancer cells to hypoxic stress, which HSFs appear to lack. This finding is in agreement with those of other studies, which have shown that post-hypoxic tumor cells have a reactive O 2 -species-resistant phenotype.35

## Discussion

Cancer cells at the core of solid tumors exist in severe hypoxic conditions. However, how these cancer cells can survive and adapt to such stressful environments remains poorly understood. In this study, we simulated this tumor core environment using a membrane-based culture system that allows metastatic prostate cancer cells to self-generate a hypoxic environment, at levels of 10 − 3 normoxic concentrations. We showed that larger cells generally move faster and have trajectories that tend to align with the self-established O 2 gradient. During hypoxia and after hypoxia was removed, the log-normal distribution of cell areas was shifted to larger sizes, even 7 days after hypoxia. These results suggest that the largest PC3 cells are more resistant to hypoxic stress, potentially moving toward higher O 2 concentrations while maintaining a low level of O 2 consumption.

Furthermore, we showed that subjecting cells to 30 h of hypoxia resulted in drastic cell loss in the severe hypoxic center of the chamber, as evidenced by a reduction in cell O 2 consumption and diffusion of O 2 into the region. Surprisingly, the log-normal cell size distribution shows that the rebounded population of cells that grew back into the previous high hypoxia region changed its size distribution to one where extremely large cells disappeared in the distribution. This suggests not only the hypoxia resistance of metastatic PC3 cells but also that PC3 large cells are more fit in the O 2 -deficient tumor sectors and ultimately evolve to a smaller phenotype after the existential threat is removed.

Together, our results demonstrate that the largest cells tend to be more resistant and adaptive to hypoxia than the smaller cells. There are several possibilities for this: (1) under severe hypoxia, a fraction of cells enter a senescent state (where they remain metabolically active but do not divide due to the danger of accumulation of genetic damage in hypoxia36), increase in nuclear area, and enter cell-cycle arrest36; (2) another possibility is that there is an already existing population of large cells, possibly polyaneuploid, that are resistant to hypoxia damage. The latter we find more likely given the immediate response of the large cells, and given that typically polyaneuploid cells undergo reductive cell division to produce cells of smaller sizes once the stressor is removed,37 although either model is possible.

### Limitations of the study

This is an in vitro study of cancer cells in self-generated hypoxia, requiring very small volumes of media. We measure O 2 levels and O 2 consumption in hypoxia, not whole-cell metabolism, which presents significant technical challenges at the microscale volumes employed. Continuous tracking of individual cells throughout the experiment via brightfield imaging would have provided invaluable insights. Furthermore, incorporating nuclear staining would have been helpful in distinguishing whether the surviving cells were pre-existing polyaneuploid populations or cells that transitioned into a senescent state during the course of the study.

Future work should aim to translate these findings to in vivo imaging experiments, such as mouse tumor models. In addition, it will be important to investigate the molecular mechanisms behind the acquisition of size-dependent survival and motility, perhaps exploring the role of hypoxia-inducible transcription factors, which are important for regulating cellular responses to hypoxia.38

### Experimental model and study participant details

#### Cell lines

PC3 cells are an epithelial cell line obtained from an advanced prostate cancer metastasis.42 We used PC3 cells expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the cytosol, allowing cells to be imaged by fluorescence microscopy. PC3-GFP cells were kindly provided by the Pienta laboratory. The PC3-GFP cell line was originally generated by labeling standard PC3 cells (ATCC, CRL-1435) with the pLenti-CMV-GFP-Neo (657-2) GFP expression vector (Addgene, Plasmid 17447).43 The HSF-GFP was kindly provided by the Pienta Laboratory and generated using pLenti-CMV-GFP-Neo (657-2) GFP expression vector (Addgene, Plasmid 17447). Selection and isolation of fibroblast-GFP+ were performed with Sony Synergy Cell Sorter separation device (Sony Biotechnology Inc., San José, CA, USA) and based on GFP expression and incorporation of Propidium Iodide (PI) for the exclusion of dead cells. PC3-GFP and HSF-GFP cells were authenticated by short tandem tepeat (STR) profiling and tested for mycoplasma contamination by the Pienta laboratory. Cells were confirmed to be mycoplasma-free before use in experiments. The cells were cultured to near surface confluence in a T-15 culture flask containing 10 mL of RPMI media (-) phenol red (Gibco, Thermofisher) containing FBS at 37 ° C . The cells were released by removal of the culture medium and adding 1 mL TrypLE-Express (Gibco, Thermofisher) at 37 ° C for 15 minutes. The TrypLE-Express was diluted by adding 5 mL of RPMI medium. 1 mL of the resulting detached cell suspension was placed in a 35 mm Lumox culture dish described below, which was mounted in a 6 well culture plate and mounted on the stage of an OkoLab incubated Nikon Eclipse TE2000-E inverted microscope.

### Method details

#### Development of phosphorescent thin film

We used a custom optically transparent O 2 -permeable thin film containing a platinum-porphyrin phosphorescent dye whose excited state is quenched by O 2 to monitor local O 2 concentrations, and upon which we cultured cells. The dye phosphorescence intensity is an easily measured function of O 2 concentration over at least 3 orders of magnitude of concentration. When used in a microfabricated 3D ecology, we obtain time and 2D space resolved hypoxia of a PC3 cancer colony. The sensor film is fabricated by dissolving Pt(II) meso-tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl) porphine (PtTFPP) into a thermal curable poly(perfluoroether) (PFPE) which is highly O 2 permeable. The sensor film was spun into a thin 100 μ m film which was then placed on a 30 mm diameter glass cover slip. The film side of the cover slip was then placed against the bottom of a 35 mm diameter gas permeable Lumox cell culture dish (Sarsteadt). The sandwich setup with the gas permeable top and gas impermeable bottom ensured that the sensor was responsive to only the self-generated hypoxia in the cell culture (Figures 1A, 1B, and 2B).

#### Experimental setup with acrylic plug

The plug placed above the cells consisted of a 5 mm thick, 25 mm diameter acrylic plug. The bottom surface of the plug was patterned with a laser-cut 100 μ m thick acrylic adhesive film (McMaster-Carr) to have a 30 mm diameter ring of 100 μ m high, and 1 mm diameter pillars spaced 2000 μ m center to center. The 100 μ m high cylinders provided a consistent head for the cells to grow and provided a time-invariant height for calculations of diffusion of O 2 in from the perimeter of the acrylic plug (Figure 1A). Note that this feature is a significant departure from recent work in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research,21 which used a cover slip with no spacer to settle over cells. In that case, there was the possibility of a time-varying media flow that could move cells, and even crush them, as the coverslip settled over the cells to presumably a very thin layer.

#### Self-generated hypoxia procedure

The 6 well plate with the cells was cultured in an on-stage CO 2 incubator at 37 ° C until full adhesion to the Lumox substrate was observed, typically after a period of 24 hours. We then over a period of 5 seconds (to minimize hydrodynamic flow) slowly lowered a sterile 30 mm diameter acrylic plug over adherent PC3 cells. Due to the 100 μ m pillar height of the bottom of the plug and the slowness of the lowering, we observed no hydrodynamic flow of media out to the edges that would detach or move the cells to the periphery, and the 100 μ m headroom ensured that the cells were not crushed by the top of the plug or forced outwards with time (Figure 1A).

#### Imaging

The application Nikon Elements Advanced Research (https://www.microscope.healthcare.nikon.com/products/software/nis-elements) was used in image stitch mode with a Plan Fluor 4X objective and an Andor Zyla cooled camera on a Nikon Eclipse TE2000-E inverted microscope. Images were taken periodically in fluorescent green GFP mode (for cell imaging) and the m-Cherry mode (for hypoxia imaging), typically every 0.5 hours. The acrylic plug could be removed at any stage of the hypoxia duration, and the adherent cells could continue to be imaged periodically to determine whether PC3 viability had been maintained after extreme self-induced hypoxia.

#### O 2 gradient calculations

Let ϕ ( x , y , t ) be the local concentration of O 2 present in the experiment as a function of spatial position ( x , y ) and time t . Here x and y are measured in μ m and t is measured in hours. Let d be the side length of a square image pixel in μ m .

Although ϕ ( x , y , t ) is not a smooth function due to the discrete pixelization of images and the 0.5 hour time intervals between images, we can still approximate its first order partial derivatives by averaging the function’s slopes between ( x , y , t ) and the relevant adjacent pixels.(Equation 9) ∂ ϕ ∂ x ≈ 1 2 ( ϕ ( x + d , y ) − ϕ ( x , y ) d + ϕ ( x , y ) − ϕ ( x − d , y ) d )

which simplifies to:(Equation 10) ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ x ≈ ϕ ( x + d , y ) − ϕ ( x − d , y ) 2 d .

The formulas for ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ y and ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ t are analogous. The magnitude of the gradient can then be calculated as: | ∇ ϕ ( x , y ) | = ( ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ x ) 2 + ( ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ y ) 2 .

Furthermore, we can approximate the second (non-mixed) partial derivatives using a Taylor series expansion: ϕ ( x + d , y ) = ϕ ( x , y ) + ∂ ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ x · d + 1 2 ∂ 2 ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ x 2 · d 2 + O ( d 3 ) .

It follows that: ∂ 2 ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ x 2 ≈ ϕ ( x + d , y ) + ϕ ( x − d , y ) − 2 ϕ ( x , y ) d 2

and the formulas for ∂ 2 ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ y 2 and ∂ 2 ϕ ( x , y ) ∂ t 2 are analogous. With these formulas it also becomes straightforward to approximate the Laplacian ∇ 2 ϕ = ∂ 2 ϕ ∂ x 2 + ∂ 2 ϕ ∂ y 2 of the O 2 distribution, which will be useful for estimating the O 2 consumption rate of the PC3 cells.

Note that while at every pixel in space we can compute the Laplacian at that pixel from the 6 surrounding values of the measured O 2 levels by taking discrete differences, in practice this is a noisy procedure. Therefore, the resulting pixel map was smoothed with a 100 μ m Gaussian filter.

#### Local O 2 concentration spatial changes

Let ϕ ˜ ( x , y , t ) be the local variation in the concentration of O 2 . We will use the sign convention that ϕ ˜ > 0 indicates that O 2 concentration has increased and ϕ ˜ < 0 indicates that O 2 has decreased. In this experiment, O 2 enters by the inwards diffusion of O 2 from the edges of the plug and is consumed by the O 2 consumption of the PC3 cells. Under the conditions of mass conservation, Fick’s second law of diffusion states that locally: ∂ ϕ ∂ t − D ∇ 2 ϕ = 0 where D is the diffusion constant of O 2 in an aqueous solution at 37 ° C, 2.644 × 10 − 5 cm 2 /sec.44 Accounting for O 2 sources (external) and sinks (cell O 2 consumption) in our experiment requires the addition of the extra term ϕ ˜ ( x , y , t ) ∂ t for the local variation in O 2 levels:(Equation 11) ∂ ϕ ∂ t − D ∇ 2 ϕ = ∂ ϕ ˜ ∂ t .

∂ ϕ ˜ ∂ t is the rate of change in O 2 density due to the O 2 consumption of PC3 cells. Let Ω be any 2D spatial region contained in the interior of the Lumox plate. We can evaluate a surface integral to calculate the total change in the amount of O 2 contained in Ω resulting from PC3 cell O 2 consumption:(Equation 12) d d t ∮ Ω ϕ ˜ d A = ∮ Ω ∂ ϕ ˜ ∂ t d A = ∮ Ω ( ∂ ϕ ∂ t − D ∇ 2 ϕ ) d A .

Alternatively, we may apply the divergence theorem to obtain:(Equation 13) d d t ∮ Ω ϕ ˜ d A = ∮ Ω ∂ ϕ ∂ t d A − D ∮ ∂ Ω ∇ ϕ · d n → .

This expression requires evaluating a line integral of the dot product of D ∮ ∂ Ω ∇ ϕ · d n → around the area Ω to obtain the net flux.

However, we can calculate the net O 2 consumption rate d O 2 d t within area Ω as the integral of the local ϕ ˜ O 2 time derivatives and the Laplacian of ϕ over the area:(Equation 14) d d t ∮ Ω ϕ ˜ d A = ∮ Ω ( ∂ ϕ ∂ t − D ∇ 2 ϕ ) d A .

The left side of Equation 14, d d t ∮ Ω ϕ ˜ d A represents the net flux of O 2 into the area encircled by the line integral. The right side is the integral over the local O 2 change. When there is a rapid change in O 2 , as determined by ∂ ϕ ∂ t , the total flux of O 2 d d t ∮ Ω ϕ ˜ d A is dominated by the time-dependent term. However, once the system reaches the quasi-steady state, the Laplacian − D ∇ 2 ϕ is the largest term. Since we are most interested in the response of the cancer cells to relatively long term and constant hypoxia, the Laplacian term is used as a proxy for local O 2 flux at steady state during severe hypoxia.

Another advantage of using − D ∇ 2 ϕ is that it provides a map of the spatially resolved local O 2 steady flux, − D ∇ 2 ϕ , and hence it carries local information about O 2 changes. Since ∇ 2 ϕ is a scalar field, it is computationally easier and more direct than computing the dot product of two vectors around a perimeter. Furthermore, it presumably is related to the local cell O 2 consumption in steady state.

However, note that − D ∇ 2 ϕ is a function of the local spatial curvature of the O 2 field that can be both positive and negative in sign; that is, apparent O 2 sources and sinks can appear in complicated environments, which are not connected to cell O 2 consumption.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Cell size determination and tracking

Time-stacked image sequences consisting of stitched separate exposures of the cells were taken in the fluorescent green GFP channel with a Plan Fluor 4x object and an Andor Zyla cooled camera on a Nikon Eclipse TE2000 inverted microscope. The contrast and brightness of the images was adjusted using the microscopy image analysis application ImageJ (https://imagej.net/ij/) to a uniform level.39 The ImageJ plugin Trackmate40 was used to analyze the image stack. Within Trackmate we used the Cellpose detector module,41 set for the cyto pretrained model since the GFP in our cells is in the cytoplasm. The cell diameter was set to 20 μ m as the initial estimation.

Once cells were identified using segmentation analysis of Cellpose, subsequent displacements of the center of mass of the cells vs. time was calculated using Trackmate (Figures 1D, 1E, 2E, 2F, 3A, and 3B). Cells whose positions could not be uniquely identified in successive frames were not included in tracking analysis. Cell speed was determined by the line integral of subsequent displacements, as opposed to cell net displacements, which use the initial and final positions of cells.

#### Distribution of PC3 cell sizes

We were interested in the influence of cell size on survival in extreme hypoxia. Cell division is a multiplicative branching process which gives rise to a predicted log-normal size distribution. A relatively simple analysis that can be performed is therefore an examination of the distribution of the sizes of the PC3 cells before, during, and after extreme hypoxia compared to a log-normal size distribution. This simple derivation is due to Herve Carruzzo (unpublished work, hcarruzz@uci.edu), a much more complete discussion of population distributions can be found in.45 The following is a very simple model which captures the basic shape of the observed distribution but leaves out other aspects which are discussed in,45 we simply attempt here to capture the basic shape of the observed distribution.

We used the area occupied by each cell in an image as a proxy for its true three-dimensional size. There are shortcomings to this proxy as the cells sometimes overlap or are cut off at the edges of the image, reducing their perceived area. However, the fraction of such cells is small (around 10 − 3 to 10 − 4 based on the sample of cells used in the image segmentation validation).

A multiplicative process can be defined as follows. Given a random variable X i which follows the same assumptions as before, we define a multiplicative process as:(Equation 15) X i = C × X i − 1 where C is a randomly distributed constant. Taking the log of both sides and applying the property of logarithms, we find:(Equation 16) log ( X i ) = log ( C i × X i − 1 ) log ( X i ) = log ( C i ) + log ( X i − 1 )

Taking an initial X 0 , we can repeat this process N times, yielding:(Equation 17) log ( X N ) = log ( C N ) + log ( C N − 1 ) + ⋯ + log ( C 1 ) + log ( X 0 ) = log ( X 0 ) + ∑ i = 1 N log ( C i )

We may now apply the central limit theorem. Since the log of a random variable is also a random variable, we now have a sum over a random variable plus some constant. We have turned a multiplicative process into an additive one. Thus, by the central limit theorem, we can see that the log of a multiplicative process tends to follow a normal distribution (Figures 2G and 2H).
